PC: Request additional information such as laboratory studies, vital signs, NPO status, PMHx, and previous anesthetic information.
Identify further strategies for IV placement including ultra-sound guidance of peripheral line or central line placement, intraosseous access, or lastly a venous cutdown.

Suggest strategies for pharmacologic assistance such as topical anesthetics (ex. EMLA cream), subcutaneously injected local anesthetics and/or with careful parenteral premedication (i.e. nasal dexmedetomidine, rectal midazolam, or IM ketamine) to successfully place IV/IO access.
Select for induction, propofol, ketamine, or etomidate as acceptable choices at reduced doses to minimize hypotension along with succinylcholine ideally (+/- atropine) or rocuronium.

Have airway equipment available in case of difficulty (i.e. Miller and/or Macintosh blades, CMAC, Glidescope, Bougie, LMAs, etc…) and demonstrate a working knowledge of the ASA difficult airway algorithm.

Treat post-induction with some or all of the following: NS or LR fluid administration, pressors as needed, head down positioning, and/or, adjusting the depth of anesthesia to not exceed 1 MAC of volatile agent (assuming the patient does not move with incision).

Suggest placing an additional IV +/- placing an arterial line in order to obtain blood for labs (at a minimum critical care Hgb and/or Hct) and for typing and screening the patient. An arterial line should be considered if frequent lab draws may potentially be required, if hemostasis proves difficult for the surgeons, and/or if hemodynamic instability is deemed to need more aggressive beat to beat monitoring than a non-invasive BP cuff can yield.
Place a gastric suction catheter and empty the stomach contents prior to extubation.
Extubate the patient once fully awake to ensure patient is able to protect their own airway which will minimize the risk of pulmonary complications
Perform an airway exam in the emergent setting
MK: Recognize the need for a rapid sequence induction and IV/IO placement prior to induction.
Identify primary versus secondary post-tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy hemorrhage
Identify expected laboratory abnormalities in an actively bleeding patient
Analyze laboratory data, patient vital signs, and physical exam to diagnose volume status
Propose goals of resuscitation including, correcting hypovolemia through administration of normal saline or lactated ringers solution, albumin, and/or the need for blood transfusion
Identify a patient who is a full stomach and at high risk for pulmonary aspiration and complications
Identify and be prepared to manage a difficult airway
SBP: Prior to induction, begin intravascular volume replacement, request that blood products be available in the operating room (initially O+ until type and screen is complete), and request that the ENT surgeon be readily available in the operating room during induction for possible surgical airway if needed.
Prior to electrocautery, the learner should decrease the inspired oxygen concentration in order to minimize potential for airway fire.
ICS: Request appropriate consultation and aid of professional colleagues such as making sure an ENT surgeon is present on induction and communicate with them the plan
PBLI: The learner is receptive to and reflects upon feedback provided following the simulation.
